compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Two learners may spend an afternoon working quietly in the same studio. The setting, task and their familiarity with the technique can explain that similarity.

The shared letters describe an inward orientation of attention, a preference for concrete information, and openness to new information in the outside world. They cannot tell you whether someone prefers making something by hand.

People can reach the same decision about a piece for different reasons. The relevant T/F distinction is the weight given to personal values or to criteria that can be applied consistently.

### ISFP and ISTP: one piece, two grounds for judging it

In a fictional studio, the rim of a cup collapses on the wheel. Two learners have the same piece, tools, time and brief. Both might decide to remake it.

One reason to remake it is that the result no longer expresses the maker’s intent. Another is that it fails a stability criterion the maker would use for any similar piece. Either ISFP or ISTP could consider both reasons.

A technically sound piece can still depart from the brief’s intention. A piece that expresses the maker’s intention can still have a technical fault. Checking both helps the maker decide what to change.

When reflecting on the choice, ask what the maker wanted to preserve and which standard the piece needed to meet. Trying, checking or setting aside the piece first cannot establish a type.

### ISFP and ISTP: why the second and third positions match while dominant and inferior differ

In type dynamics, the shared I and P place the perceiving process in the outward-facing auxiliary position. The shared S makes that process extraverted Sensing (Se). Changing F to T changes the inward-facing dominant from Fi to Ti and the inferior from Te to Fe. Both have tertiary Intuition.

Within the model, Fi weighs how well a choice accords with personal values. Ti weighs whether the reasoning is internally consistent. In the studio example, those lenses can help someone distinguish the maker’s intent from a standard for evaluating the method. Neither lens substitutes for skill.

The Foundation’s overview lists tertiary Intuition as Ne or Ni for both ISFP and ISTP. This page uses Ni for both, and the dominant and auxiliary descriptions remain the same. See the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

(Fictional example) Two learners are eight weeks into the same technique and have the same practice hours. One asks whether a finished piece expresses the intended design. Another uses the same criteria to assess whether the result holds up across comparable practice pieces. Either type can use both checks.

A finished piece can show whether the overall design works. A record of comparable attempts can show where results vary. Reviewing both can help a learner choose what to practise next.

Record one decision you made, which criteria mattered and what would change your mind. The notes can help you understand what you value in the work, without determining type.

### ISFP and ISTP: the portfolio review, and which piece to change

(Fictional example) Two people review the same five-piece portfolio under the same submission rules and deadline. One concern is whether a praised piece still expresses the maker’s intention. Another is whether that piece meets the same technical standard as the rest. Either type can raise both concerns.

Before revising, check which criteria the panel will use and which details matter most to the maker. Where the brief requires sound construction, personal expression and construction quality both need a place in the decision.

An ISTP can revise an acceptable piece because it misses the intended effect. An ISFP can address a technical flaw. A revision by itself cannot establish type.

(Fictional example) Two learners receive a new instructor’s explanation of the same technique. They can ask whether the new approach suits their design and whether its reasoning accounts for what they observe. Either type can ask both questions.

Two comparable samples can help the learners see what changes, provided they have a permitted, low-risk way to make them. Compare the results against the same brief and discuss unexplained differences with the instructor.

Follow the studio’s operating procedures and get qualified supervision for equipment or work with little room for error. A low-risk paper mock-up can show whether a changed shape still serves the intended design.

### ISFP and ISTP: one old piece of furniture left by the parents

(Fictional scene) The old flat is being given up and the wooden table in the living room, thirty years old, cannot simply be carried out. Condition, available space, budget and moving constraints are the same for both: scratches on the top, one loose joint, a narrow doorway.

Two questions belong in the decision: what the table means to the family, and whether it meets the same practical standards they would apply to any table they planned to keep. Either person can weigh sentimental value, repair costs and space.

Check whether it fits and obtain a repair estimate before deciding. Those facts establish what is feasible. The family still decides how much the table’s history matters to them.

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Two learners may spend an afternoon working quietly in the same studio. The setting, task and their familiarity with the technique can explain that similarity.

The shared letters describe an inward orientation of attention, a preference for concrete information, and openness to new information in the outside world. They cannot tell you whether someone prefers making something by hand.

People can reach the same decision about a piece for different reasons. The relevant T/F distinction is the weight given to personal values or to criteria that can be applied consistently.

### ISFP and ISTP: one piece, two grounds for judging it

In a fictional studio, the rim of a cup collapses on the wheel. Two learners have the same piece, tools, time and brief. Both might decide to remake it.

One reason to remake it is that the result no longer expresses the maker’s intent. Another is that it fails a stability criterion the maker would use for any similar piece. Either ISFP or ISTP could consider both reasons.

A technically sound piece can still depart from the brief’s intention. A piece that expresses the maker’s intention can still have a technical fault. Checking both helps the maker decide what to change.

When reflecting on the choice, ask what the maker wanted to preserve and which standard the piece needed to meet. Trying, checking or setting aside the piece first cannot establish a type.

### ISFP and ISTP: why the second and third positions match while dominant and inferior differ

In type dynamics, the shared I and P place the perceiving process in the outward-facing auxiliary position. The shared S makes that process extraverted Sensing (Se). Changing F to T changes the inward-facing dominant from Fi to Ti and the inferior from Te to Fe. Both have tertiary Intuition.

Within the model, Fi weighs how well a choice accords with personal values. Ti weighs whether the reasoning is internally consistent. In the studio example, those lenses can help someone distinguish the maker’s intent from a standard for evaluating the method. Neither lens substitutes for skill.

The Foundation’s overview lists tertiary Intuition as Ne or Ni for both ISFP and ISTP. This page uses Ni for both, and the dominant and auxiliary descriptions remain the same. See the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Two learners may spend an afternoon working quietly in the same studio. The setting, task and their familiarity with the technique can explain that similarity.

The shared letters describe an inward orientation of attention, a preference for concrete information, and openness to new information in the outside world. They cannot tell you whether someone prefers making something by hand.

People can reach the same decision about a piece for different reasons. The relevant T/F distinction is the weight given to personal values or to criteria that can be applied consistently.

### ISFP and ISTP: one piece, two grounds for judging it

In a fictional studio, the rim of a cup collapses on the wheel. Two learners have the same piece, tools, time and brief. Both might decide to remake it.

One reason to remake it is that the result no longer expresses the maker’s intent. Another is that it fails a stability criterion the maker would use for any similar piece. Either ISFP or ISTP could consider both reasons.

A technically sound piece can still depart from the brief’s intention. A piece that expresses the maker’s intention can still have a technical fault. Checking both helps the maker decide what to change.

When reflecting on the choice, ask what the maker wanted to preserve and which standard the piece needed to meet. Trying, checking or setting aside the piece first cannot establish a type.

### ISFP and ISTP: why the second and third positions match while dominant and inferior differ

In type dynamics, the shared I and P place the perceiving process in the outward-facing auxiliary position. The shared S makes that process extraverted Sensing (Se). Changing F to T changes the inward-facing dominant from Fi to Ti and the inferior from Te to Fe. Both have tertiary Intuition.

Within the model, Fi weighs how well a choice accords with personal values. Ti weighs whether the reasoning is internally consistent. In the studio example, those lenses can help someone distinguish the maker’s intent from a standard for evaluating the method. Neither lens substitutes for skill.

The Foundation’s overview lists tertiary Intuition as Ne or Ni for both ISFP and ISTP. This page uses Ni for both, and the dominant and auxiliary descriptions remain the same. See the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

sections.body_md:
All four examples are fictional. They illustrate possible trade-offs and cannot establish how often either type behaves a certain way. Follow studio procedures and qualified supervision when using equipment.

When two people disagree about a revision, ask what they want the piece to express and what technical requirement it must meet.

### ISFP and ISTP: learning a skill alone, and what counts as knowing it

(Fictional example) Two learners are eight weeks into the same technique and have the same practice hours. One asks whether a finished piece expresses the intended design. Another uses the same criteria to assess whether the result holds up across comparable practice pieces. Either type can use both checks.

A finished piece can show whether the overall design works. A record of comparable attempts can show where results vary. Reviewing both can help a learner choose what to practise next.

Record one decision you made, which criteria mattered and what would change your mind. The notes can help you understand what you value in the work, without determining type.

### ISFP and ISTP: the portfolio review, and which piece to change

(Fictional example) Two people review the same five-piece portfolio under the same submission rules and deadline. One concern is whether a praised piece still expresses the maker’s intention. Another is whether that piece meets the same technical standard as the rest. Either type can raise both concerns.

Before revising, check which criteria the panel will use and which details matter most to the maker. Where the brief requires sound construction, personal expression and construction quality both need a place in the decision.

An ISTP can revise an acceptable piece because it misses the intended effect. An ISFP can address a technical flaw. A revision by itself cannot establish type.

### ISFP and ISTP: changing teacher or tool, and how to compare two accounts

(Fictional example) Two learners receive a new instructor’s explanation of the same technique. They can ask whether the new approach suits their design and whether its reasoning accounts for what they observe. Either type can ask both questions.

Two comparable samples can help the learners see what changes, provided they have a permitted, low-risk way to make them. Compare the results against the same brief and discuss unexplained differences with the instructor.

Follow the studio’s operating procedures and get qualified supervision for equipment or work with little room for error. A low-risk paper mock-up can show whether a changed shape still serves the intended design.

### ISFP and ISTP: one old piece of furniture left by the parents

(Fictional scene) The old flat is being given up and the wooden table in the living room, thirty years old, cannot simply be carried out. Condition, available space, budget and moving constraints are the same for both: scratches on the top, one loose joint, a narrow doorway.

Two questions belong in the decision: what the table means to the family, and whether it meets the same practical standards they would apply to any table they planned to keep. Either person can weigh sentimental value, repair costs and space.

Check whether it fits and obtain a repair estimate before deciding. Those facts establish what is feasible. The family still decides how much the table’s history matters to them.
